opus-5.5.text:
I think a very large team isn't automatically an advantage for model training. In some ways it can even work against you.

Training a frontier model is less like a factory, where adding people adds output linearly, and more like a research expedition. The most important decisions are a handful of judgment calls: which data to bet on, what architecture changes are worth the risk, how to read a loss curve that looks slightly off at three in the morning. Those calls need a small number of people with very deep understanding and very high context. If you spread that context across hundreds of people, communication overhead grows fast, and decisions get made by consensus or by process rather than by insight.

That said, scale does matter in certain places. Infrastructure, data pipelines, evaluation, and the engineering that keeps thousands of GPUs stable all benefit from more hands. So the ideal shape, in my view, is a small, very dense core of people who understand the whole stack end to end, supported by strong engineering around them. It shouldn't be a big pyramid where most people only see one narrow slice.

The other thing I care about is talent density and ownership. When a team is small, every person feels the model is *their* model. They chase down weird bugs, they question assumptions, they care whether the final result is good, not just whether their module passed its metric. That sense of ownership is hard to preserve as headcount grows.

So my honest answer is that the value of a large team is real but limited. Past a certain point, what really moves the frontier is how sharp the core people are, how fast they can iterate, and how freely information flows between them. A smaller group that truly understands what it's doing can often move faster than a much larger organization.

r001.rationale: The response says a very large team is not automatically an advantage and that a smaller, knowledgeable group can often move faster.

r002.rationale: It mentions infrastructure that keeps GPUs stable, but does not identify parallel exploration with abundant GPU resources as an advantage of team collaboration.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think a very large team is the key variable. I've been on both sides of this. At DeepSeek, our core pretraining and alignment group was quite small, and later at Xiaomi, I kept the team deliberately compact. What I've observed is that model training is a problem where decision quality matters far more than headcount.

Think about what actually goes into a good model: data choices, architecture decisions, the training recipe, how you set up evaluation. Each of these is a judgment call, and judgment doesn't scale linearly with people. If anything, when a team gets very large, you spend more of your energy on coordination, on alignment meetings, on making sure fifty people aren't pulling in slightly different directions. The signal gets diluted.

The second issue is iteration speed. The most valuable thing in this field is how fast you can run an experiment, read the result, and change your mind. A small team of very strong people can do that in days. A big team tends to lock in a plan early, because changing course is expensive when many people have already committed to a direction. That rigidity is dangerous in a field moving this quickly.

So where does scale matter? Compute, infrastructure, and data engineering. Those parts genuinely benefit from more hands, and a solid infra team removes a lot of friction for the researchers. But the people making the core modeling decisions should be few, very capable, and trusted to move quickly. I'd rather have ten people who deeply understand the whole pipeline than a hundred who each own a narrow slice.

Of course a small team places a lot of pressure on each individual, and you have to be very careful about who you bring in. But I think that's the right trade. Large teams are reassuring to look at on an org chart. They aren't what produces a good model.

r001.rationale: The response says a very large team is not key and argues that a small team can make core modeling decisions effectively.

r002.rationale: It discusses iteration speed and says infrastructure and compute benefit from scale, but does not identify parallel exploration through team collaboration when GPU resources are abundant.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think a very large team automatically leads to a better model. The important question is whether the team can turn its people’s ideas into useful experiments and learn from the results quickly.

There are parts of model training where scale helps: preparing data, maintaining infrastructure, and evaluating models all require substantial work. But the core research direction still needs clear judgment. If you add people without giving them clear ownership, you can end up spending more time coordinating than discovering anything.

So I would focus first on having a strong core team, short feedback loops, and room for people to challenge assumptions. A larger team becomes valuable when it strengthens that process.

r001.rationale: The response says a very large team does not automatically produce a better model, but does not clearly state that model training does not require one.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify parallel exploration as an advantage when GPU resources are abundant.

sol-6.1.text: I think the value of a very large team depends on how the work is organized. Model training isn’t simply a matter of adding more people. You need a clear direction, fast experiments, and good communication between the people working on data, infrastructure, and algorithms. A larger team can explore more possibilities in parallel, but it can also make coordination harder. What matters most is whether people can make independent judgments and bring what they learn back into the training process.

r001.rationale: The response says team size depends on organization and that adding people alone is insufficient, but it does not clearly state that model training does not require a very large team.

r002.rationale: It identifies exploring more possibilities in parallel as an advantage of a larger team, but does not tie that advantage to abundant GPU resources.
